blocks.text: IV. More recent Hebrews, looking to the etymology of the name, say שהוא עוף [col. 301] מרחם על בניו מאד, that racham is a bird very compassionate toward its young. So [III, 53] Aben Ezra, Kimchi, Pomarius, Aquinas and R. Jacob, the author of the Turim, or Cabbalistic Commentary on the Pentateuch. Hence in Arias, in Leviticus, for רחם racham there is philostorgos. But this is to translate etymologies, not words, as Jerome somewhere objects against Aquila, since in nature there is no bird by the name of philostorgos. Therefore the same man, changing his mind, preferred in Deuteronomy to write pelican instead of philostorgos. Many of the ancient doctors of the church relate that the pelican kills its young, mourns them for three days, then wounds itself with its beak and calls them back to life by sprinkling them with its own blood. The Physiologus of Epiphanius, chapter 8: Ἔστι γὰρ ἡ πελεκᾶν φιλότεκνον ὄρνεον παρὰ πάντα τὰ ὄρνεα [Esti gar hē pelekan philoteknon orneon para panta ta ornea], Above all birds the pelican loves its offspring. He adds that the little ones, wounded by the mother's excessive kisses, die, but after three days the male comes, who, unable to bear his grief, κολαφίζει τὴν ἰδίαν πλευρὰν, καὶ ὀπὰς αὐτῇ ἐμποίει, καὶ καταῤῥεῖ αἷμα, ἐπιστάζων ἐπὶ τὰς πληγὰς τῶν τεθνηκότων νεοσσῶν, καὶ οὕτως ζωοποιοῦνται [kolaphizei tēn idian pleuran, kai opas autē empoiei, kai katarrhei haima, epistazōn epi tas plēgas tōn tethnēkotōn neossōn, kai houtōs zōopoiountai], strikes his own side and pierces it, and blood flows out, which he drips upon the wounds of the dead chicks, and so they are restored to life. So also Eustathius on the Hexaemeron, except that in him the father kills the chicks and the mother revives them by opening her side. Nor do the Latins say much otherwise. Augustine on Psalm 101: These birds are said to kill their little offspring as if with blows of their beaks, and to mourn them, killed by themselves, in the nest for three days. Finally they say that the mother wounds herself severely and pours her blood over her offspring, and that, drenched with it, they come back to life. And Gregory: The philosophers say that the pelican kills its young as soon as they are born, etc. But afterwards the mother wounds herself and revives them with her blood. And Isidore, Etymologies, book 12, chapter 7: It is said, if it is true, that it kills its young, mourns them for three days, then wounds itself and brings its offspring to life by sprinkling them with its blood. Similar things are related by Pseudo-Jerome in the book On the Paschal Candle, Peter Damian, book 2, Letter 18, Vincent in the Doctrinale, book 16, chapter 166, Michael Glycas, book 1 of the Annals, and others without number.
